I've been farming this same land in Quzhou my whole adult life. Thirty years teaches you what works here. My 3 mu splits naturally: 2 mu for the wheat-maize rotation — wheat in winter, maize on the same ground right after harvest in summer — and 1 mu for cotton. Cotton earns more cash per mu, but it demands more work and more spraying, so I don't expand it. With some of my family earning wages in town, I need the cotton income to balance the household.

For wheat, I plant in early October like everyone around here. I buy improved Jimai seed from the village supply shop — reliable, and I know what to expect. I till with the rotary machine before sowing. I apply compound fertilizer as base and urea when the plants are jointing in spring. I irrigate three times: once before sowing to settle the seedbed, once at jointing, once at heading. I spray twice — once for aphids in spring, once for powdery mildew if it comes.

For maize, I plant within a day or two of the wheat harvest in June so I don't waste the season. Hybrid seed, everybody uses hybrid now. I apply base fertilizer at planting and top-dress urea when the plants reach knee height. If July is dry, I pump from the well twice; if rain is decent, once is enough. Usually one pesticide spray for corn borer.

For cotton, I deep plough in March to loosen the soil — cotton roots go deep. I transplant seedlings in late April. Cotton needs the most attention: more fertilizer spread across the season, more pesticide for bollworm and aphids. I irrigate four times from May through August. This is the hardest crop but it earns cash we need.
